builder_plan.scenario: Tool errors or unavailable services cause your agent to abandon recoverable tasks.
builder_plan.change: Inject repeatable tool failures and change only the recovery policy.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current retry and fallback behavior under the same injected failures.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Recovered tasks, duplicate side effects, retries, time to recovery, and total cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Repairs for Whom? Evaluator-Executor Mismatch in Selecting Repairs for Failed LLM Agents
summary: The method replaces scoring candidate repairs with greedy replay, a stronger proxy model, an environment oracle, or a log-reading judge, instead selecting repairs using rollouts from the agent that will actually execute them. The cost is rollout budget for the deployed policy at selection time, though the paper reports that twenty 14B rollouts per candidate are worth no more than two of the 7B agent's own rollouts, so the approach can be cheaper than proxy-model scoring while being more accurate. It can fail when own-policy rollouts are unavailable or too expensive, when the deployment policy changes after repair labels are created (invalidating executor-specific labels), and when the failure set was pre-screened for repair value, a regime the paper does not test.
rationale: The finding is directly actionable for constrained infrastructure since the deployed small model's own rollouts outperform a larger proxy scorer at equal or lower cost, but the evidence covers only ALFWorld and WebShop with specific model pairs, so the reader should validate the executor-mismatch effect on their own agent and repair pipeline before adopting it as standard practice.
technique: Executor-matched repair selection via own-policy rollouts

claims.statement: The method replaces scoring candidate repairs with greedy replay, a stronger proxy model, an environment oracle, or a log-reading judge, instead selecting repairs using rollouts from the agent that will actually execute them. The cost is rollout budget for the deployed policy at selection time, though the paper reports that twenty 14B rollouts per candidate are worth no more than two of the 7B agent's own rollouts, so the approach can be cheaper than proxy-model scoring while being more accurate. It can fail when own-policy rollouts are unavailable or too expensive, when the deployment policy changes after repair labels are created (invalidating executor-specific labels), and when the failure set was pre-screened for repair value, a regime the paper does not test.

Greedy replay loses 0.08-0.13 expected net success gain in ALFWorld and 0.06-0.13 net reward in WebShop versus selection with the deployed agent's own rollouts; selecting repairs for Qwen2.5-7B with Qwen2.5-14B rollouts loses 0.25 in ALFWorld and 0.07 in WebShop, and cross-family evaluators lose 0.07-0.17 in both directions.
